nexusClaim.associationBasis: Social phobia is near-universal in selective mutism and is the single best-established associated condition, with two independent designs reporting very high rates: a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 eligible studies (N=837) pooled the prevalence of comorbid anxiety disorders in selective mutism and found that 80 percent of children with selective mutism carried an additional anxiety disorder, NOTABLY SOCIAL PHOBIA AT 69 PERCENT, while reporting considerable heterogeneity that remained unexplained by a priori specified moderators and concluding that the disorders are NOT DISCRETE, SEPARABLE CATEGORIES (PMID 31650460); and a comparative behavioral study of 95 children and adolescents with selective mutism against 74 with social phobia, 46 with other internalizing disorders, and 119 typically developing controls, using the Child Behavior Checklist with diagnostic-interview comorbidity assessment, found social phobia detected in 94 PERCENT of children with selective mutism while showing that the two groups differ, with selective mutism more frequently carrying lifetime separation anxiety disorder (45 versus 26 percent) and oppositional defiant disorder (22 versus 5 percent) and LESS frequently carrying generalized anxiety disorder (6 versus 20 percent) and major depression (12 versus 26 percent) (PMID 27089281); a parent-reported clinical characterization of 230 children with diagnosed or suspected selective mutism reports that anxiety AND SOCIAL ANXIETY SYMPTOMS WERE ELEVATED, with age of onset and diagnosis both earlier than previously reported and an average diagnostic delay of 2 years (PMID 37650960); recorded as documented association only, with the near-ubiquity of the co-diagnosis explicitly framed as challenging the separability of the two diagnoses rather than as establishing a route between them.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the located evidence is better read as a challenge to the diagnostic boundary than as a causal claim: the meta-analysis states explicitly that the finding that selective mutism is often diagnosed in combination with anxiety disorders indicates that these disorders are NOT DISCRETE, SEPARABLE CATEGORIES, and that this finding DOES NOT ELUDICATE the relation between selective mutism and anxiety as an aetiological mechanism OR AS A SYMPTOMATIC FEATURE, so the co-occurrence cannot be used to argue that one produces the other. The meta-analysis also carries considerable heterogeneity that remained unexplained, so its 69 percent social-phobia figure is a pooled estimate with real between-study spread, and its own stated recommendation is that research strategies for assessing anxiety be broadened before the relationship is classified. The comparative study establishes a diagnostic overlap, not an aetiology. Individual claims require a dated social anxiety disorder diagnosis with documented fear of social evaluation, a dated selective mutism diagnosis documenting speech absence in specific social contexts with normal speech in others, and a clinical determination of which diagnosis is primary, because at a 94 percent co-detection rate the two diagnoses are frequently recorded as alternatives for the same presentation rather than as separate conditions in one patient.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is a shared social-evaluative fear circuit in which anticipation of negative evaluation in a speaking situation produces an inhibition of vocalization that is specific to social contexts, so that the child speaks normally with familiar people and falls silent with peers, which is the defining observation of the disorder; the mechanism is named as a shared circuit rather than a causal sequence because the located evidence cannot separate whether the social fear recruits the mutism, the mutism itself generates and then reinforces social fear through the child's experience of being unable to speak, or both are expressions of one underlying social-evaluative vulnerability, and the meta-analysis expressly declines to resolve that question.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at meta-analytic, comparative-cohort, and parent-report-characterization class, following the file's existing psychiatric, neuropsychiatric, medication-related, and sleep-related pathway scope: the meta-analysis is the anchor that supplies the pooled 80 percent additional-anxiety-disorder and 69 percent social-phobia figures together with the explicit non-separability statement and the unexplained heterogeneity (PMID 31650460); the comparative study is the anchor that supplies the 94 percent co-detection rate and, importantly, the DIFFERENTIAL PROFILE showing selective mutism carries more separation anxiety and oppositional defiant disorder but LESS generalized anxiety disorder and major depression than social phobia, which is what makes the two diagnoses distinguishable rather than interchangeable (PMID 27089281); and the parent-report characterization supplies the contemporary presentation and the 2-year average diagnostic delay, which is the located reason a benefits record may contain one diagnosis where the other was the presenting concern (PMID 37650960). Because the evidence is a challenge to categorical separability rather than a causal route, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, quotes the non-separability statement directly in the causation status, and requires dated separate diagnoses with a primary-determination before any individual attribution.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The primary anchor is a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 studies with 837 children that reports CONSIDERABLE HETEROGENEITY remaining unexplained by a priori specified moderators, so its 69 percent social-phobia figure should be read as a pooled estimate with real between-study spread rather than a precise rate, and the authors state the finding does not elucidate aetiology or symptomatic relationship; the comparative study is a single multi-group cohort of 95 selective-mutism participants drawn from specialist settings, so its 94 percent co-detection rate is enriched for referred cases and is not a community prevalence; the parent-report characterization of 230 children includes both diagnosed and SUSPECTED cases, which dilutes the specificity of its findings; NO located anchor establishes temporal order between the two diagnoses; and no located anchor reports how many children with both diagnoses have a documented primary diagnosis, which is the quantity an individual claim needs. Notably, the SAME comparative anchor reports that children with selective mutism were LESS affected by generalized anxiety disorder than those with social phobia (6 versus 20 percent), so the broad anxiety-disorder route was withheld as EVIDENCE-CONTRADICTED-ON-ITS-OWN-ANCHOR rather than authored. The depressive-disorder route was withheld as CHAIN-CONFLICT, since the registry already carries social-anxiety-disorder to depressive-disorder and a direct selective-mutism to depressive-disorder edge would duplicate a relationship this file's rank 1 edge already implies.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Separation anxiety is markedly over-represented in selective mutism relative to its comparison group, which is the located evidence that distinguishes the two anxiety phenotypes rather than collapsing them: the comparative behavioral study of 95 children and adolescents with selective mutism against 74 with social phobia found that selective-mutism participants were MORE FREQUENTLY AFFECTED BY LIFETIME SEPARATION ANXIETY DISORDER, 45 PERCENT AGAINST 26 PERCENT, while simultaneously being less affected by generalized anxiety disorder and major depression, so the two conditions present different comorbidity profiles (PMID 27089281); the same profile is what makes selective mutism separable from social phobia rather than a variant of it, since the two diagnoses load on different additional conditions (PMID 27089281); a family-accommodation study of 38 children with selective mutism, 28 with selective mutism plus comorbid anxiety disorders, 34 with other anxiety disorders, and 30 with non-anxiety disorders found that accommodation in the selective-mutism sample was prevalent though reported at lower frequency and with lower parental distress than expected, with NO CORRELATION between accommodation and selective-mutism symptom severity (PMID 40586947); and the 230-child parent-reported characterization reporting elevated anxiety and social anxiety symptoms supplies the contemporary presentation context (PMID 37650960); recorded as documented association only, with the reverse-and-parallel nature of the relationship disclosed.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the direction of the relationship is genuinely unresolved: both conditions are childhood anxiety diagnoses recorded concurrently, the located comparative study reports LIFETIME separation anxiety disorder in 45 percent of children with selective mutism but does not establish whether the separation anxiety preceded the mutism, followed it, or was diagnosed alongside it, and a lifetime prevalence figure is by construction uninformative about sequence. A substantial diagnostic component is likely, since a child who cannot speak to a parent on school morning is difficult to distinguish from a child with separation distress, and the located family-accommodation anchor makes the reverse direction concrete: parental accommodation is described as a maintaining factor in the selective-mutism picture, which is a parent-to-child process that could equally intensify separation distress. The family-accommodation study also reports NO CORRELATION between accommodation and symptom severity, which is a direct null against the assumption that accommodation severity tracks illness severity. Individual claims require dated, separately signed diagnoses of both conditions with the chronology established, and clinician determination of whether the two diagnoses describe one presentation or two conditions.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is a shared separation-related fear circuit in which distress at separation from a caregiver generates both the somatic and emotional symptoms of separation anxiety and a narrowing of situations in which the child will speak, so that the mutism becomes most pronounced precisely in the school-separation contexts where the separation anxiety is most activated; the mechanism is named as shared rather than sequential because the located evidence reports concurrent lifetime diagnoses without establishing order, and because a bidirectional maintaining loop is at least as plausible, in which separation anxiety drives school refusal which reinforces the mutism, and the mutism which is experienced as failure reinforces the separation distress.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at comparative-cohort, family-accommodation, and parent-report-characterization class, and registered as rank 2 rather than rank 1 on the located evidence: the 45 percent lifetime separation-anxiety figure is markedly lower than the 94 percent social-phobia co-detection rate at this file's rank 1 edge, and the honest ordering reflects that (PMID 27089281). The comparative study is the anchor that supplies both the 45-versus-26-percent contrast and the contrasting generalized-anxiety and depression figures that make the two anxiety phenotypes distinguishable (PMID 27089281); the family-accommodation study is registered as the anchor that documents a MAINTAINING-FACTOR mechanism running in the reverse direction, and specifically for its null on the correlation between parental accommodation and symptom severity (PMID 40586947); and the 230-child parent-report characterization supplies the contemporary presentation context (PMID 37650960). Because the relationship is concurrent and possibly bidirectional, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, states the unresolved direction in the causation status, quotes the accommodation null openly, and requires dated separate diagnoses with chronology before any individual attribution.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The primary anchor is a single multi-group specialist cohort of 95 children with selective mutism, and the figure is a LIFETIME prevalence, which cannot order the two diagnoses in time; that cohort is drawn from specialist settings and is enriched for referred and comorbid cases; the family-accommodation study has small diagnostic-group samples (38, 28, 34, 30) drawn from a single private practice intake stream, which is a highly selected sample, and its central null, that no correlation was found between accommodation and symptom severity, should not be read as evidence that accommodation is unimportant, only that this sample did not demonstrate the correlation; the 230-child parent-report characterization includes suspected as well as diagnosed cases; NO located anchor reports whether separation anxiety is temporally antecedent, consequent, or concurrent in any individual; and no located anchor reports a selective-mutism-free comparison group for the separation-anxiety outcome, so the 45-versus-26-percent contrast is against a social-phobia group rather than against unaffected children. The depressive-disorder route was withheld as CHAIN-CONFLICT against the registered social-anxiety-disorder to depressive-disorder edge, and the generalized-anxiety-disorder route was withheld because this file's own anchor reports LESS of it, not more.

School refusal arising from separation distress rather than from a selective-mutism diagnosis, which are overlapping but distinct presentations
